latin: Circiter CCXX (ducentae viginti)<sup>1</sup> naves eorum paratissimae atque omni genere armorum ornatissimae, e portu profectae<sup>2</sup>, nostris adversae constiterunt.

Neque satis Bruto, qui classi praeerat*, neque tribunis militum centurionibusque, quibus singulae naves erant attributae<sup>3</sup>, constabat quid agerent aut quam rationem pugnae insisterent<sup>4</sup>.
Una erat magno usui res praeparata a nostris: falces<sup>5</sup> praeacutae, insertae adfixaeque longuriis<sup>6</sup>, non absimili<sup>7</sup> forma muralium<sup>8</sup> falcium.
His, cum funes, qui antemnas<sup>9</sup> ad malos<sup>10</sup> destinabant, comprehensi adductique erant, navigio remis incitato, praerumpebantur<sup>11</sup>.
Quibus abscissis<sup>12</sup>, antemnae necessario concidebant<sup>13</sup>, ut, cum omnis gallicis navibus spes<sup>14</sup> in velis armamentisque consisteret,
his ereptis omnis usus navium uno tempore eriperetur<sup>15</sup>.
Reliquum<sup>16</sup> erat certamen positum in virtute, qua nostri milites facile superabant...
Disjectis<sup>17</sup>, ut diximus, antemnis, cum<sup>18</sup> singulas binae ac ternae naves circumsteterant, milites summa vi transcendere in hostium naves contendebant.
Quod<sup>19</sup> postquam<sup>20</sup> barbari fieri* animadverterunt, expugnatis compluribus navibus, cum ei rei nullum reperiretur auxilium, fuga salutem petere contenderunt<sup>21</sup>.
Ac jam conversis in eam partem navibus quo ventus ferebat*, tanta subito malacia<sup>22</sup> ac tranquillitas exstitit<sup>23</sup>, ut se ex loco movere non possent*.
Quae quidem res ad negotium conficiendum maxime fuit opportuna,
nam singulas nostri consectati<sup>24</sup> expugnaverunt, ut perpaucae noctis interventu ad terram pervenerint, cum ab hora fere quarta<sup>25</sup> usque ad solis occasum pugnaretur.
english: About 220 of their ships, [in excellent condition] (very prepared) and [perfectly] (very) equipped with weapons of every sort, having come out of the port, took up position [opposite] ours.

Neither Brutus, who commanded the fleet, nor the [military] tribunes and the centurions, to whom each one of the ships had been assigned, [saw clearly] (satis constabat) what they should do, or [on] what method of combat they should rely.
There was one thing [of] great usefulness prepared by our men: well-sharpened scythes, fitted and fixed to long poles, of a form not different [from that] of [siege] scythes (murales).
By means of these [scythes], when the ropes which held the yards to the masts had been caught and pulled towards oneself, the ship being driven [by force] of oars, they were cut.
[When] these [ropes] were cut, the yards inevitably fell, so that, as all hope for the Gallic vessels lay in the sails and in the [rigging] (armamentis),
once these were taken away, all usefulness of the ships was taken away [at a single stroke] (time).
[The rest] (remaining) [of the] combat rested on courage, in which our soldiers easily [had the upper hand] (dominated)...

[Once] the yards [were] dislocated as we have said, when [each ship found itself surrounded by two or three of ours] (ships two by two and three by three had surrounded them one by one), the soldiers strove to pass forcibly into the ships of the enemies.
After the barbarians noticed that this was happening (thus), [and that] several ships [had been] put out of action, as no help could be found [for this], they sought to gain [safety] by flight.

And already the ships having turned [in the direction] (in that part) where the wind was carrying, there suddenly arose such a calm and such tranquillity that they could not move from the spot [where they were].
And certainly, this circumstance was very favourable for finishing the enterprise,

for our men [followed them] and took them one by one, so that very few reached land [thanks to the] (by) [coming] of night, when one had fought from about [ten o'clock in the morning] (the fourth hour) until sunset.

footnotes: CCXX = 220. One still finds so-called Roman numerals in classical works. As soon as it is a question of large numbers, one must recognize that it is not really practical! In fact the Roman men of action had more efficient and faster systems which, unfortunately, we know imperfectly. But that is another story! If we do not know them, you will find the way of using so-called Roman numerals in any classical grammar.

Profectae, perfect participle f. pl. of proficiscor (L. 44, N. 11). — Adversae, p.p.p. of advertere, to turn towards. Adversus is also an adverb, meaning against, facing, and is constructed with the accusative.
Tribunus militum, colonel in the army, transformed here, for the needs of the cause, into captain of a vessel! Same remark for the word centurio, which designates a junior officer of the land army.
Insisto, -is, -ere, stiti, v.i., to stand upright on..., to lean on... (here subj. impf.).

Falx, falcis, f., the scythe. Nouns ending in the nominative singular in two consonants or in a double consonant (x = cs) are generally feminine (trabs, urbs, etc.) but the exceptions are numerous: fons, pons, dens, grex, etc.
Longurium, -ii, n., long pole (longus, -a, -um, long).
Absimilis = dissimilis.
Muralis, -is, -e, relating to the wall, to the rampart (murus, -i, m.); here, siege equipment.
Antemna, -ae, f., here the word is taken in its first sense: yards, that is to say pieces of wood intended to hold the sails; the antenna of the insect and the radio antenna are derived senses.
Malus, -i, m., mast (a long). Not to be confused with malus, -i, f., the apple tree (a also long), nor with malum, -i, n., the apple; nor with malus, -a, -um, bad (a short).
Praerumpere, to break by the end (prae, prep. + abl., in front).
Abscido, -is, -ere, scidi, scisum, to separate by cutting (caedere, to cut).
Concido, -is, -ere, cidi, no supine, to fall at a stroke (cadere, to fall).
Spes, spei, f. (5th decl.), hope (epithet: omnis, three words before).
Eripio, -is, -ere, ripui, reptum, to take away (ex + rapere).
Reliquus, -a, -um, that which remains (cf. French relique).

Disjectis: Other editions than the one we have followed carry dejectis (or respectively disiectis and deiectis). The first is the perfect passive participle of disjicere, to dislocate; the second is the perfect passive participle of dejicere, to throw down. Both come from jacere, jacio, jeci, jactum (to throw), which must not be confused with jacere, jaceo, jacui (to be lying). — If you read the Bellum Gallicum in a serious edition, such as the one we indicate in the Bibliographical Index, you will find there mention of the variants of the different manuscripts, and the preface will give you information on the fascinating question of the origin of the text you will have before your eyes.

Cum, conj.: 1° TEMPORAL SENSE: when; it is constructed with the indicative, as is the case in phrase 8. — 2° CAUSAL SENSE (even if the relation of time is partially preserved): as, because; it is then constructed with the subjunctive. E.g.: cum id animadvertisset (subj. pluperfect) fugit, as he had noticed it, he fled (cum is here causal, and not only temporal, for if he had not noticed anything, he would have stayed); likewise (P. 9), cum nullum reperiretur (subj. imperfect passive) auxilium.
Quod (of P. 9) is a simple relative, moreover in correlation with ei (cf. is... qui, ea... quae, id... quod); subject of fieri (w. f. w., that to be done), this P. 1. being object of animadverterunt.
Postquam is constructed with the indicative; but antequam (before) follows the same rule as cum (cf. note 18 above and GRAMMATICAL APPENDIX).
Contendo, -is, -ere, tendi, tentum, to stretch towards..., to try to...
Malacia, -ae, f. (Greek origin), calm, that is to say calm of the sea; the opposite of the storm, tempestas (cf. L. 50, N. 1) or procella.
Exsisto, -is, -ere, stiti, to rise from, to show oneself, to become, to exist.
(Con)sectari, to follow (cf. French secte).

Hora quarta: The day, from sunrise to sunset, was divided into twelve equal hours, but whose duration necessarily varied according to the season: the fourth hour therefore began at the start of the third third of the morning (10 o'clock at the equinox). As for the worker of the eleventh hour, he was the one who presented himself for work an hour before sunset.
comments: Trieris, -is, f., or triremis, -is, f., trireme (Athenian) or trireme (Roman): galley with three banks of oars. — Carthago, -inis, f., Carthage, mortal enemy of Rome. The Carthaginians: Poeni, -orum, m., whence the adjective punicus, -a, -um, Carthaginian; fides punica, Carthaginian good faith, that is to say bad faith, for the Romans, who often broke their given word, accused the Carthaginians of never keeping it. — Lagona = lagoena; note e (ex) lagona and not ad lagonam (obvious logical reason). — Plebs, plebis, f., the people, the plebs; here instead of populus, for reasons of rhythm. — Navarchus, -i, m. (word of Greek origin), he who commands (archos) the ship (naus). — Securis, -is, f., the axe: belongs to the nouns that have the accusative in im and the ablative in i (like vis, turris, etc.). — Gladius, -ii, m., the sword, here the (boarding) sabre.

In this poem, which is Virgilian only in inspiration (!), do not try to retain the order of the words: versifiers often permit themselves a few fancies! Likewise the strong beat of the melody does not always correspond to the grammatical tonic accent marked in bold.

english: [Towards the end of the month of August] (the sun was turning towards September)
— when we saw a trireme
— which, having left the Carthaginian land
— was cleaving the salty foam (the foams of salt):
— it was heading for Sicily (Trinacria).
Refrain: We must drink [from] (out of) the bottle!
— Drink to the lovers!
— To the health of the Roman Senate
— and of the people (plebs). The Carthaginians, though, (to the bad gallows)
— may they all go [to the devil]!
When the captain saw the Carthaginians,
— he calls us to boarding.
— With the ram we stove in the trireme.
— With the axe and with the sabre, those people,
— we sent [them] down to the underworld.
